subject: Culture
title: Sitting Shiva
description: A micro-lesson that makes Sitting Shiva usable.

hook.text: In Jewish tradition, mourners sit on low chairs for seven days while the community brings food and comfort.

buildup.text: Shiva strips normal life away: no work, no entertainment, no personal grooming. Grief gets full priority.

discovery.text: The community's role is defined precisely. Visitors should not speak until the mourner speaks first.

twist.text: Judaism structures grief in stages: seven days of shiva, thirty days of shloshim, then eleven months of kaddish.

climax.text: The graduated system prevents both suppression and wallowing. Grief is managed, not ignored or indulged.

punchline.text: The best grief systems know that pain needs a timeline, not a cure.

quiz.question: How long does the shiva mourning period last?

details.summary: Sitting shiva is the Jewish mourning period where the bereaved spend seven days at home receiving visitors, covering mirrors, and sitting on low chairs. This structured grief practice provides community support while giving mourners explicit permission to stop functioning normally.
details.whyItMatters: Shiva demonstrates how structured mourning rituals provide both emotional support and social permission to grieve. Psychologists increasingly recognize the therapeutic wisdom embedded in this ancient practice.
takeaways: Shiva lasts seven days following burial
Mourners sit on low chairs and cover mirrors in the home
The community is obligated to visit and provide food

faq.question: What are the rules for sitting shiva?
faq.answer: During shiva's seven days, mourners stay home, sit on low chairs or the floor, cover mirrors, avoid bathing for pleasure, do not wear leather shoes, and refrain from work. Visitors bring food so mourners need not cook. A minyan (ten people) gathers daily for prayer.

faq.question: Why do mourners cover mirrors during shiva?
faq.answer: Several explanations exist: vanity and self-focus are inappropriate during mourning; prayer should not be recited facing a reflected image; and the soul of the deceased might become trapped in the mirror.
